modules.name: Nucleophilic Substitution of Haloalkanes and Haloarenes

blocks.title: Core Concept
blocks.text:
Nucleophilic Substitution Reactions of Haloalkanes

Nucleophilic Substitution of Haloalkanes and Haloarenes

SN1 Mechanism (Unimolecular Nucleophilic Substitution):

$\text{1st step: Formation of a carbocation (rate-determining step)} \\ \text{R--X} \xrightarrow{\text{Slow, rds}} R^+ + X^- \\  \text{2nd step: Attack by the nucleophile} \\ R^+ + \text{Nu}^- \xrightarrow{\text{Fast}} R\text{--Nu}$

Characteristics of SN1 Reaction:

  • Two-step reaction involving carbocation formation.
  • Rate: Rate=k[Alkyl halide], order and molecularity = 1.
  • The rate is independent of the nucleophile's concentration.
  • A carbocation intermediate is formed; rearrangement is possible.
  • Favoured by polar protic solvents (e.g., H₂O, ROH).
SN2 Mechanism (Bimolecular Nucleophilic Substitution Reaction)

$R-X + \text{Nu}^- \rightarrow R-\text{Nu} + X^-$

Characteristics of SN2 Reaction:

  • Single-step reaction with simultaneous bond breaking and forming.
  • Rate: $\text{Rate} = k[\text{Alkyl halide}][\text{Nucleophile}]$
  • so order and molecularity = 2.
  • The rate depends on the concentration of the nucleophile.
  • No carbocation intermediate; hence, no rearrangement occurs.
  • Favoured by polar aprotic solvents (e.g., DMSO, DMF, acetone).

blocks.title: Data
blocks.text:
Difference between SN1 and SN2

SN1

  • SN1 reaction is favored by a poor nucleophile (H2O, ROH)
  • SN1 reaction is favored in polar protic solvent
SN2

  • SN2 reaction is favored by high concentration of a good nucleophile (Anionic nucleophiles)
  • SN2 reaction is favored in polar aprotic solvent
Reactions of Haloalkane

blocks.title: Example-1
blocks.question:
Which type of solvent favors the $ S_N1$ mechanism?

a) Non-polar solvent
b) Polar protic solvent
c) Polar aprotic solvent
d) Any type of solvent
blocks.answer:
Answer: b) Polar protic solvent
Explanation: Polar protic solvents stabilize the carbocation intermediate and the leaving group, facilitating the $ S_N1 $reaction.

blocks.title: Example-2
blocks.question:
Consider the reaction,

CH3CH2CH2Br + NaOH →   CH3CH2CH2OH + NaBr

This reaction will be fastest in:-

(1) Water

(2) Ethanol

(3) Methanol

(4) N, N'-dimethylformamide (DMF)
blocks.answer:
Answer: (4) N, N'-dimethylformamide (DMF)

Explanation: The reaction follows the $S_N2$ mechanism, favoured by polar aprotic solvents like DMF. These solvents do not form hydrogen bonds with the nucleophile, allowing it to remain free and highly reactive, thus increasing the reaction rate.

blocks.title: Common Mistakes
blocks.text:
• Confusing between SN1 (unimolecular) and SN2 (bimolecular) mechanisms.
  • Ignoring steric factors that affect SN2 reactions.
  • Overlooking the role of solvents (polar protic for SN1, polar aprotic for SN2).
  • Forgetting that haloarenes are less reactive due to resonance stabilization.

blocks.title: Points to Remember
blocks.text:
• Electron withdrawing groups present at ortho-para position with respect to the leaving group increase the rate of reaction.
  • Aryl halide without electron-withdrawing substituents doesn’t react with most nucleophiles under ordinary conditions.

blocks.title: Example-1
blocks.question:
What are the major products formed when chlorobenzene undergoes nitration using a mixture of concentrated $HNO_3 ~and~ H_2SO_4$ ?

a) 1,3 Dinitrobenzene

b) m- Nitrochlorobenzene

c) p- Nitrochlorobenzeneonly

d) Amixture of  o- Nitrochlorobenzene  p- Nitrochlorobenzeneonly
blocks.answer:
Answer: d) A mixture of  o- Nitrochlorobenzene  p- Nitrochlorobenzeneonly

Explanation:

This reaction is an Electrophilic Aromatic Substitution. The chlorine atom is an ortho, para-directing group, guiding the incoming nitro group {NO_2^+}$ to these positions. This results in a mixture of o-Nitrochlorobenzene and p-Nitrochlorobenzene.

  • Forgetting that halogens deactivate the benzene ring towards electrophilic substitution.
  • Misunderstanding the mechanism of nucleophilic substitution in haloarenes.
  • Confusing the reactivity of different halogen-substituted haloarenes.

blocks.title: Example-2
blocks.question: Which of the following compounds (a) and (b) will not react with a mixture of NaBr and H2SO4?
blocks.answer: Ans. Compound (b) (phenol) will not react because the -OH group on the benzene ring is stabilized by resonance and cannot be replaced under the given conditions. Compound (a) (propanol) reacts as its -OH group is on an aliphatic chain, which can undergo substitution.

blocks.title: Example-3
blocks.question:
What is the product of the Sandmeyer reaction involving benzene diazonium chloride and CuCl?

a) Chlorobenzene
b) Benzyl chloride
c) Methyl chloride
d) Ethyl chloride
blocks.answer:
Answer: a) Chlorobenzene
Explanation: In the Sandmeyer reaction, benzene diazonium chloride reacts with CuCl to form chlorobenzene.

blocks.title: Common Mistakes
blocks.text:
• Confusing the preparation methods for haloalkanes (e.g., free radical halogenation) with those for haloarenes (e.g., halogenation via electrophilic substitution).
  • Overlooking the required conditions, like temperature and reagents, for specific reactions.
  • Forgetting the difference between alkyl and aryl halides in reactivity and preparation methods.

blocks.title: Core Concept
blocks.text: Note: Grignard reagent behaves like a base (reacts with compounds containing acidic H) as well as like a nucleophile.

blocks.title: Example
blocks.question:
Choose the incorrect statements about the Grignard reagent.

a) Grignard reagents (RMgBr) are reagents that add to the carbonyl group of aldehydes and ketones.

b) An organosodium compound is not very reactive as compared to a Grignard reagent.

c) Grignard reagents can be prepared in ether or tetrahydrofuran (THF).

d) Water and alcohol decompose Grignard reagents.
blocks.answer:
Answer: b) An organosodium compound is not very reactive as compared to a Grignard reagent.

Explanation: Organosodium compounds (RNa) are generally less reactive than Grignard reagents (RMgBr). Grignard reagents are highly reactive due to the polar nature of the C−Mg bond, making them more nucleophilic.
blocks.prompt:

b) An organosodium compound is not very reactive as compared to a Grignard reagent.

c) Grignard reagents can be prepared in ether or tetrahydrofuran (THF).

d) Water and alcohol decompose Grignard reagents.

blocks.title: Common Mistake
blocks.text:
• Forgetting that they must be prepared in anhydrous conditions to avoid hydrolysis.
  • Not recognizing their strong nucleophilic nature and reactivity with electrophiles.
  • Overlooking the importance of Grignard reagents in forming carbon-carbon bonds.
